source.title: How Can Increased Randomness in Stochastic Gradient Descent Improve Generalization?
source.authors: Arwen Bradley; C. Gomez-Uribe; Manish Reddy Vuyyuru

record.file_problem: The supplied full text is present. Some equations and symbols are visibly corrupted or flattened by extraction, but the main result descriptions and experiment text are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests related generalization and SGD-noise claims using train/test loss, curvature, and temperature experiments; it does not test the catalog versions' specified memorization, width, architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness-measure, or memorized-example claims directly.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's reported experiments that measure train/test performance, train/test shift, curvature, or SGD temperature. Cited findings from other work and values appearing only in figures are not reconstructed as numerical results. Synthetic basin examples are reported as explicit textual results, but do not bear on a listed version.
record.test_reason: Appendix G.1 directly bears on V5: VGG9 is trained for the same 1000 additional epochs across batch sizes and learning rates. Test loss improves with learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio, and scaling learning rate with batch size approximately preserves performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify shift-, bias-, and covariance-curvature contributions to approximate test loss and find substantial empirical shift-curvature contributions. Their steady-state analysis predicts a depth-versus-curvature trade-off in an effective potential. Its assumptions and extension requiring modified SGD in the overparameterized case qualify that theoretical conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes curvature and SGD's steady-state distribution and reports CIFAR10 temperature and train/test-shift experiments; it does not reproduce the interventions or measurements specified in the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: For VGG16, shift magnitude increased with temperature; for Resnet10 it decreased. In the CIFAR10 VGG9 temperature experiment, test loss decreased with temperature while train loss stayed roughly constant; small batches (50 and 100) had higher train loss under some second-stage settings, which the authors attribute to mismatched batch-normalization statistics and parameters. Reshuffling the CIFAR10 split had little impact, while smaller sample sizes increased test loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher initial SGD temperature accompanies lower directional curvature and shift-curvature in VGG16 and Resnet10; shift magnitude changes in opposite directions across the architectures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Directional shift-curvature helps approximate test loss at train minima in these CIFAR10 experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Reshuffling train/test membership has little effect on loss, whereas smaller samples increase test loss while training loss stays small.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The experiments are consistent with finite sampling contributing to train/test differences in CIFAR10.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed loss landscapes show beneficial or harmful temperature effects depending on the arrangement of basin depths and widths.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the theoretical steady-state distribution, temperature's effect on test loss depends on basin geometry and train/test shift.

record.problems: The empirical curvature experiments use CIFAR10 VGG16 and Resnet10, estimate curvature with one-dimensional symmetrized quadratic fits rather than full Hessians, and provide mainly qualitative results in the supplied text. The VGG9 temperature experiment uses a two-stage procedure and reports final loss as the median of the last 100 steps. The theoretical steady-state analysis relies on diffusion and Gaussian-mixture approximations and assumes steady state; the authors note limitations for overparameterized models and near-zero-curvature directions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Numerical values shown only in Figures 1–6 were not reconstructed from plots; the text reports the qualitative findings recorded above.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance compared with natural labels.
Width increases beyond interpolation and their effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and sensitivity to tuning.

Training from scratch across batch sizes, a critical batch-size threshold, language models, and remedies involving longer training, warmup, or changed regularization. The batch comparison here concerns continued training from a converged large-batch initialization.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V5. R3 already captures the relevant qualitative findings, so no missing-result entry is needed, but it should be divided into fixed-learning-rate and matched-temperature comparisons. No plotted numerical losses were inferred.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label memorization or natural-label generalization comparison.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold test.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps.

rows.subject: VGG16
rows.operation_detail: Measured train/test loss and curvature along the line joining train and test local minima across initial SGD temperatures.

conditions.value: range of temperatures; exact values not stated in the main experiment description

rows.measure: Train loss and test loss at local minima; train/test curvature along the connecting line; shift magnitude and shift-curvature.
rows.value: Test loss at the train minimum was approximately the test loss at the test minimum plus shift-curvature; train and test curvature and shift-curvature decreased with increasing temperature. Shift magnitude increased with temperature.
rows.note: The text reports qualitative trends, not the listed claim versions' outcomes. VGG16 shift magnitude behaved differently from Resnet10.
rows.check: Directional quadratic-fit curvature and shift-curvature do not measure V7's magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance or its ranking of generalization gaps. Initial training epochs also vary inversely with temperature, so this is not a fixed-epoch batch comparison.

rows.subject: Resnet10
rows.size_stated: Resnet16 implementation modified by reducing blocks per group from 3 to 2
rows.operation_detail: Measured train/test loss and curvature along the line joining train and test local minima across initial SGD temperatures.

conditions.value: range of temperatures; exact values not stated in the main experiment description

rows.measure: Train loss and test loss at local minima; train/test curvature along the connecting line; shift magnitude and shift-curvature.
rows.value: Test loss at the train minimum was approximately the test loss at the test minimum plus shift-curvature; train and test curvature and shift-curvature decreased with increasing temperature. Shift magnitude decreased with temperature.
rows.note: The text reports qualitative trends, not the listed claim versions' outcomes. Train curvature exceeded test curvature for Resnet10.
rows.check: Directional quadratic-fit curvature and shift-curvature do not measure V7's magnitude-aware sharpness. Initial training epochs vary inversely with temperature. The architecture modification is correctly transcribed, although the stated Resnet10 name and block count warrant preserving the authors' description.

rows.subject: VGG9
rows.operation_detail: Continued training from a converged large-batch initialization for 1000 epochs at varied batch sizes and learning rates, varying temperature.

conditions.value: large batch size 4096; decreasing learning-rate schedule
learning rate divided by batch size; from 2.44e-8 to 2.44e-5

rows.measure: Final train loss and test loss; median of last 100 steps, with mean and standard deviation across trials.
rows.value: Test loss decreased with increasing temperature while train loss remained roughly constant; both depended primarily on temperature. At the end of stage one, mean final train loss = 0.005 (var 4e-07) and test loss = 0.555 (var 1e-4).
rows.uncertainty: Mean and standard deviation across 10 trials; stage-one variances stated as above.
rows.note: The figure's temperature-specific plotted values are not stated in text. The end-of-stage-one values are textual setup context, not a separate intervention result row.
rows.check: This is a fixed-epoch batch-size experiment bearing on V5, despite its temperature framing. At fixed learning rate, larger batches mean lower temperature and higher test loss; proportional learning-rate scaling approximately preserves loss across batches. Split these comparisons into separate rows. Small batches 50 and 100 have elevated training loss at small learning rates, attributed to batch-normalization mismatch. The hyperparameter table specifies momentum 0.9 in stage one and 0 in stage two; the prose's blanket no-momentum description is inconsistent with that table.

rows.subject: VGG9
rows.operation_detail: Retrained after merging, reshuffling, and randomly splitting the CIFAR10 train and test sets.

conditions.value: same as initial stage of temperature experiment

rows.measure: Final train/test loss under different reshufflings.
rows.value: No significant difference in test loss across different reshufflings of train and test sets.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence that distribution shift is not present in the default split.
rows.check: The absence of a reshuffling effect is not absence of any listed version's effect. The dedicated hyperparameter table gives batch size 3000, 2000 epochs, and momentum 0, differing from the temperature experiment's initial stage; retain this discrepancy rather than describing the recipes as identical.

rows.subject: VGG9
rows.operation_detail: Trained on proportional train/test splits of subsamples of different sizes.
rows.measure: Test loss and train loss as sample size varied.
rows.value: Test loss increased as sample size decreased while train loss stayed small.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative trend only.
rows.check: A sample-size effect does not test any listed version. The dedicated Figure 5 right hyperparameters differ from the temperature experiment's initial stage.

rows.measure: Expected train and test loss as temperature varies.

rows.note: A synthetic theoretical example, not a test of the catalog versions.

relationships.condition: VGG9 on CIFAR10; fixed learning rate; 1000 additional epochs after converged large-batch training.
relationships.reason: R3 reports lower test loss at higher temperature consistently across batch sizes; at fixed learning rate this means smaller batches perform better.
relationships.display_finding: Test loss was lower with smaller batches at a fixed learning rate, but this comparison remains unverified.

relationships.condition: VGG9 on CIFAR10; learning rate scaled with batch size to preserve temperature; equal additional epoch budgets.
relationships.reason: R3 and Figure 5 report approximately similar test loss at matched temperature across batch sizes, supporting V5's recipe-adaptation qualification.
relationships.display_finding: Test loss was similar when learning-rate scaling preserved temperature, but this comparison remains unverified.
